title: Do only zero and five at the end work for five?
description: Tens and ones are split apart to see why zero and five at the end make a number of fives, and why every other ending leaves a gap. Keeko then links the idea to the idli-vada game of the book, where the vada calls are five, ten, fifteen and twenty.
teaching_notes: One idea: tens are always whole fives, so only the ones digit can leave a gap. Watch for students who check only one direction of the statement.

source: Consider this statement: Numbers that are divisible by 5 are those that end with either a '0' or a '5'. Do you agree?
video_script.why: The child checks the statement in both directions by splitting a number into tens and ones.
video_script.substitution: Split a number into tens and ones, and see which last digits leave nothing over after fives are taken out.
video_script.anchor: a number split into a block of tens and a block of ones, with every ten cut into two fives
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, we agree with the statement

final_answer.value: Yes, a number is divisible by 5 exactly when its last digit is 0 or 5
final_answer.spoken: yes, a number is divisible by five exactly when its last digit is zero or five

maths_rules: each ten is 2 fives, so any number of tens is a number of fives
the last digits 0 and 5 are whole numbers of fives: 0 = 0 x 5 and 5 = 1 x 5
the last digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6, 7, 8, 9 leave 1, 2, 3 or 4 over
so 5 divides a number exactly when its last digit is 0 or 5
video_script.design: One idea: tens are whole fives, so only the last digit decides. Assumes place value and the count of fives. Real life: the vada calls of the idli-vada game. The split number stays on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, take a number that ends in five, such as three hundred and ninety five.
Split it into three hundred and ninety, and five.
<bookmark mark='tens'/>The tens make seventy eight fives.
<bookmark mark='five'/>The last five is one more five, so five divides the number.

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step two, take a number that ends in seven, such as three hundred and ninety seven.
Split it into three hundred and ninety, and seven.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>The tens are whole fives. Seven holds one five and two more.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Two is left over, so five does not divide the number.

narration: <bookmark mark='zero'/>Step three, look at every last digit from zero to nine.
Zero holds no five, and five holds one five. Both leave nothing over.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Every other digit leaves one, two, three or four over.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes, we agree; a number is divisible by 5 exactly when its last digit is 0 or 5
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes, we agree with the statement.
A number is divisible by five exactly when its last digit is zero or five.

<bookmark mark='digits'/>The last digits go five, zero, five, zero.
A child who hears a number ending in zero or five knows that five divides it.
